attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The claim is about the best results reported at the reveal on ARC and FrontierMath. 'Truly impressive' is evaluative and is correctly set aside.

contract.note: The plain reading (large jumps over the previous best on both benchmarks at the reveal) is ordinary and fair. It is scoped to the reported December results, which is what he described.

evidence.note: The benchmark owner's report gives o3's verified ARC-AGI-1 semi-private scores at the reveal: 75.7% and 87.5% (high compute).
Same report gives the earlier baseline: GPT-4o at 5% in 2024. This shows a step change. The baseline covers GPT-family models only.
Same-day reporting: 25.2% on FrontierMath against no other model above 2%. The figure is from OpenAI's internal evaluation, which fits a claim about reported demo results.
A later Epoch retest of the released o3 scored about 10%. That was a different model version and problem set, so it does not bear on what the reveal reported.

reviews.rationale: At the reveal, o3's reported ARC-AGI-1 score (75.7%, verified by ARC Prize) was far above the earlier GPT baseline (5%). Its reported FrontierMath score (25.2%) was more than ten times the prior best (2%). Both count as major advances. The later lower FrontierMath retest used a different model version and problem set, so it is context only.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: He states that the model revealed on 20 Dec 2024 was not GPT-5. The proposition matches.

contract.note: The plain reading is that OpenAI presented o3 as distinct from GPT-5. That is fair and ordinary.

evidence.note: Same-day report: OpenAI unveiled o3 as the successor to o1, not as GPT-5.
OpenAI's own later GPT-5 launch page says GPT-5 replaces o3, which confirms they are separate models. This is a company disclosure dated after the claim period.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from the reveal shows OpenAI presented the model as o3, the o-series successor to o1, not as GPT-5. OpenAI's August 2025 launch of GPT-5 as a separate model that replaced o3 confirms the distinction.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Are going to' is an unqualified forecast that many influencers will claim AGI in 2025. 'Maybe some companies' is hedged and is correctly treated as optional.

contract.note: He gave no threshold for 'a lot' and no prominence bar for 'influencer'. The contract's reading (numerous distinct, established commentators affirming that AGI has arrived) is fair, but the result turns on it.

evidence.note: Tyler Cowen, a prominent commentator, says outright in April 2025 that o3 is AGI. One qualifying instance.
Emad Mostaque in July 2025: 'AGI is already here', with a qualification that the parts still need assembling. A partial instance.
Janus asserts gpt-4o is AGI (Aug 2025). The post had low views, so the account's prominence is not established.

reviews.rationale: The 2025 horizon has passed. The packet documents one to three qualifying 2025 claims that AGI had arrived, one of them qualified. That does not establish 'a lot' of influencers. Nor is there a comprehensive record showing such claims were isolated. The evidence does not settle the forecast either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A universal negative: no outsider had evaluated o3's robustness across problem types by the post date. Faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'different types of problems' as different domains fits his context (effective in some domain, not others). He also earlier noted Chollet's single-task testing as an exception. Fair, but the result turns on that reading.

evidence.note: Live blog from the day: external safety testing of full o3 was still to come. It cannot exclude earlier private testing.
ARC Prize confirms it tested o3-preview externally in Dec 2024, but only on ARC. That is not a cross-domain robustness evaluation under the contract.

reviews.rationale: The only external testing shown before the post is ARC Prize's single-benchmark evaluation, which does not count as cross-domain robustness under the contract. But no comprehensive record of private external access exists, so the universal negative cannot be confirmed. The evidence settles the claim neither way.
